exams.title: Temperature and sales
exams.equation: Predicted daily sales = b₀ + b1[Max temperature]

variables.name: Daily sales
variables.desc: total net sales for the day ($)

questions.prompt: Predict daily sales for a day with max temperature = 70.
questions.explain: Substitute into the model: 2725.29 + (7.5797 × 70) = 3255.87.

questions.prompt: By how much do predicted daily sales change when max temperature is 10 °F higher?
At the 5% significance level, is max temperature statistically significant in this model?
questions.explain: Its p-value is 0.008, which is below 0.05, so we reject the hypothesis that its coefficient is zero.

questions.prompt: What share of the variation in daily sales does this model explain? Give R² as a percentage (one decimal).
questions.explain: R² = 0.0227, so the model explains 2.3% of the variation.

exams.title: Last year's sales and game days
exams.equation: Predicted daily sales = b₀ + b1[Sales one year ago] + b2[Game day] + b3[Sales one year ago × Game day]

variables.name: Daily sales
variables.desc: total net sales for the day ($)

variables.name: Sales one year ago
variables.desc: sales on the same weekday 364 days earlier ($)

variables.name: Game day
variables.desc: 1 = university football game that day, 0 = no game (reference group)

table.term: Sales one year ago × Game day

questions.prompt: Predict daily sales for a day with sales one year ago = 3000, game day = 1.
By how much do predicted daily sales change when sales one year ago is $1,000 higher for a day without a game (game day = 0)?
At the 5% significance level, is sales one year ago × game day statistically significant in this model?
questions.explain: Its p-value is 0.946, which is above 0.05, so we cannot reject the hypothesis that its coefficient is zero.

questions.prompt: On a game day, by how much do predicted sales change for each $1 higher sales one year ago?
questions.explain: On a game day the slope is b1 + b3 = 0.6196 + (0.0107) = 0.6303.
